claims.source: We used an antibody against the cleaved form of Death caspase-1 (Dcp-1), an effector caspase, to detect apoptotic cells (Akagawa et al., 2015) and, indeed, observed a significant increase in the number of Dcp-1 positive cells in the lamina when EGFR signalling was blocked in the xgO (132.8 cells/unit volume±19.48 standard error of the mean) compared to controls (49.14 cells/unit volume±4.53) (Figure 2A–B and D, p<0.0005, Mann-Whitney U-test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A-B and D.

claims.claim: Dcp-1 positive cells are observed in the proximal row of the lamina when EGFR signalling is blocked in xgO, which is never observed in controls.
claims.source: Importantly, we observed Dcp-1 positive cells in the proximal row of the lamina (Figure 2B; Nexp = 20/20), which we never observed in controls (Figure 2A, Nctrl = 19/19).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: EGFR activity in xgO induces the differentiation of L5 neurons, and proximal LPCs that fail to receive appropriate cues from xgO die by apoptosis.
claims.source: Altogether these results showed that EGFR activity in xgO induces the differentiation of L5 neurons, and proximal LPCs that fail to receive appropriate cues from xgO die by apoptosis.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Photoreceptor-derived EGF is required for L5 differentiation.
claims.source: We took advantage of a mutant for rhomboid 3 (rho3) in which photoreceptors are specified but cannot secrete EGF from their axons (Yogev et al., 2010), resulting in failure of L1-L4 neurons to differentiate along with a significant decrease in the number of L5s (Figure 3A and C; prho3 <0.0001; one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test) (Fernandes et al., 2017; Yogev et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and C using rho3 mutants.

claims.claim: Restoring Rho3 expression only in photoreceptors in rho3 mutant animals fully rescues L5 neuronal differentiation.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we restored expression of wild-type Rho3 only in photoreceptors in rho3 mutant animals using a photoreceptor-specific driver (GMR-Gal4). Rho3 function in photoreceptors was sufficient to fully rescue not only L1-L4 neuronal differentiation, as previously reported (Yogev et al., 2010), but also L5 neuronal differentiation (Figure 3B and C; one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: xgO likely respond to EGF from photoreceptors and relay these signals to induce differentiation of proximal LPCs into L5 neurons.
claims.source: Since photoreceptor-derived EGF was insufficient to induce L5 neuronal differentiation when EGFR signalling was blocked in xgO (Figure 1F and H), together these results suggest that xgO likely respond to EGF from photoreceptors and relay these signals to induce differentiation of proximal LPCs into L5 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Blocking EGFR signalling in xgO leads to reduced levels of double phosphorylated MAPK (dpMAPK) specifically in the proximal lamina.
claims.source: Previously, we showed that MAPK signalling is necessary and sufficient for neuronal differentiation in the lamina (Fernandes et al., 2017). Therefore, we reasoned that xgO-derived differentiation signal(s) must activate MAPK signalling through a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) in the proximal lamina. Indeed, blocking EGFR signalling in xgO led to reduced levels of double phosphorylated MAPK (dpMAPK) specifically in the proximal lamina (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: Co-expressing PntP1 with EGFRDN in xgO rescues the number of L5s per column.
claims.source: To validate this approach, we tested whether autonomously restoring transcriptional activity downstream of MAPK in xgO while blocking EGFR activity could rescue L5 differentiation. While blocking EGFR in xgO resulted in laminas containing 0.063±0.014 L5s per column, co-expressing PntP1 with EGFRDN in xgO rescued the number of L5s per column to 0.213±0.025 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C ****p<0.0001 compared to EGFRDN alone).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Spi, Branchless (Bnl), Thisbe (Ths), and Col4a1 produced statistically significant rescues of L5 differentiation when co-expressed with EGFRDN in xgO.
claims.source: We then screened 18 RTK ligands based on available reagents (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). Four ligands, Spi, Branchless (Bnl), Thisbe (Ths), and Col4a1, produced statistically significant rescues when compared with the xgO>EGFRDN + CD8::GFP (Gal4 titration control) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; *p<0.05, **p<0.005, ***p<0.0005, ****p<0.0001 one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: bnl-Gal4 drives expression in all cells of the optic lobe.
claims.source: Using a previously validated bnl-Gal4 (Chen and Krasnow, 2014; Kamimura et al., 2006; Spéder and Brand, 2014; Tamamouna et al., 2021), we drove CD8::GFP expression and found that it was expressed in all cells of the optic lobe (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), making it unlikely to be a viable hit.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: ths-Gal4 drives expression in photoreceptors but not xgO.
claims.source: We found that a previously validated ths-Gal4 (Anllo and DiNardo, 2022; Wu et al., 2017) drove CD8::GFP expression in photoreceptors but not xgO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) consistent with previous reports (Franzdóttir et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and citations.

claims.claim: Col4a1-Gal4 drives expression in xgO.
claims.source: However, when we examined Col4a1 expression using a previously validated Gal4 enhancer trap (Hennig et al., 2006), we found that it drove CD8::GFP expression in xgO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: spi-Gal4 (NP0289-Gal4) drives expression in xgO.
claims.source: We also found that a spi-Gal4 (NP0289-Gal4; not previously validated) drove CD8::GFP expression in xgO, but not photoreceptors or other cell types where spi is also known to be expressed, suggesting that this Gal4 line may report spi expression partially (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: spi and Col4a1 mRNAs are present in xgO under physiological conditions.
claims.source: To further substantiate these results we performed fluorescence in situ hybridisation chain reaction (HCR), a form of fluorescent in situ hybridisation (Choi et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2016; Duckhorn et al., 2022), and confirmed that spi and Col4a1 mRNAs were present in the xgO under physiological conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I; see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ HCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I.

claims.claim: Spi and Col4a1 rescued L5 differentiation when co-expressed with EGFRDN in xgO.
claims.source: This enabled us to narrow down our hits to two ligands: the EGF Spi and Col4a1, a type IV Collagen, which both rescued L5 differentiation resulting in laminas with 0.147±0.024 and 0.17±0.0197 L5s per column, respectively (Figure 3F–K and P pspi-wt <0.01 and pCol4a1 <0.0005, one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3F-K and P.

claims.claim: xgO are capable of processing mSpi into the active form (sSpi).
claims.source: Note that expressing either sSpi or wild-type (unprocessed) mSpi (referred to as Spiwt) in xgO rescued L5 numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), indicating that xgO are capable of processing mSpi into the active form (sSpi).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Spi expression in xgO does not autonomously rescue dpMAPK nuclear localisation in xgO when EGFR signalling is blocked.
claims.source: We ruled out the trivial explanation that the rescue of L5 numbers by Spi was caused by autocrine EGFR reactivation in the xgO, as Spi expression in xgO did not autonomously rescue dpMAPK nuclear localisation in xgO when EGFR signalling was blocked (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, J, K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, J, K.

claims.claim: Disrupting EGFR signalling in xgO results in significantly reduced fluorescence signal for spi and Col4a1 transcripts in xgO.
claims.source: We measured spi and Col4a1 transcript levels using in situ HCR in controls and when we blocked EGFR signalling in xgO. Disrupting EGFR signalling in xgO resulted in a significantly reduced fluorescence signal for spi and Col4a1 transcripts in xgO compared with controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I, 1L-O; pspi <0.01, pCol4a1<0.005; Mann-Whitney U-test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, I, L-O.

claims.claim: xgO express spi and Col4a1 in response to EGFR activity.
claims.source: Thus, xgO express spi and Col4a1 in response to EGFR activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Ddr-Gal4 drives expression in all LPCs.
claims.source: We used a Gal4 enhancer trap in the Ddr locus (not previously validated) to drive CD8::GFP expression and observed that GFP was expressed in all LPCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1P).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1P.

claims.claim: Ddr is expressed throughout the lamina.
claims.source: We confirmed these results using in situ HCR, which also detected Ddr expression throughout the lamina (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ HCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q.

claims.claim: LPCs express the RTKs that make them competent to respond to Spi and Col4a1 produced by xgO.
claims.source: Spi activates EGFR (Sopko and Perrimon, 2013), which was shown to be expressed in LPCs previously (Huang et al., 1998). Thus, LPCs express the RTKs that make them competent to respond to the EGF Spi and Col4a1 produced by xgO.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the expression patterns and previous literature.

claims.claim: Expressing spi or Col4a1 in xgO in which EGFR signalling was blocked rescued dpMAPK signal in L5s.
claims.source: Moreover, expressing spi or Col4a1 in xgO in which EGFR signalling was blocked rescued dpMAPK signal in L5s, indicating that, when expressed in xgO, these ligands were sufficient to activate MAPK signalling in the proximal lamina (Figure 3—figure supplement 1R-T; **p<0.005, ****p<0.0001; one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1R-T.

claims.claim: Co-expressing Spi and Col4a1 in xgO>EGFRDN background led to an enhanced rescue of L5 differentiation relative to individual ligand rescues.
claims.source: Co-expressing Spi and Col4a1 in the xgO>EGFRDN background led to an enhanced and statistically significant rescue relative to individual ligand rescues alone, resulting in laminas with 0.267±0.025 L5s per column (Figure 3L–P; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3L-P.

claims.claim: Overexpressing Spi in xgO results in a 19%±1.8 increase in the number of L5s per column relative to controls.
claims.source: We also tested whether these ligands could induce ectopic L5 differentiation when overexpressed in the xgO. Overexpressing either Spi or Col4a1 resulted in a 19%±1.8 (p<0.05) and a 24%±4 (p<0.005) increase in the number of L5s per column relative to controls, respectively (Figure 3Q–S).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3Q-S.

claims.claim: Overexpressing Col4a1 in xgO results in a 24%±4 increase in the number of L5s per column relative to controls.
claims.source: Overexpressing either Spi or Col4a1 resulted in a 19%±1.8 (p<0.05) and a 24%±4 (p<0.005) increase in the number of L5s per column relative to controls, respectively (Figure 3Q–S).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3Q-S.

claims.claim: Spi and Col4a1 from xgO are sufficient to induce L5 differentiation.
claims.source: Thus, Spi and Col4a1 from xgO are sufficient to induce L5 differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: Knocking down Col4a1 in xgO leads to a statistically significant decrease in L5s.
claims.source: We used RNA interference (RNAi) to knock down spi and Col4a1 expression both individually and simultaneously in xgO using previously validated lines (Chen et al., 2016; Csordás et al., 2020; Louradour et al., 2017; Morante et al., 2013; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011). While knocking down spi led to a mild decrease in L5 numbers, which was not statistically significant, knocking down Col4a1 in the xgO led to a statistically significant decrease in L5s (0.78±0.03 L5s per column) relative to controls (0.92±0.02 L5s per column) (Figure 3T, U and W; *p<0.05 one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3T, U and W.

claims.claim: Knocking down both spi and Col4a1 simultaneously in xgO leads to a strong decrease in L5s.
claims.source: However, knocking down both spi and Col4a1 simultaneously in xgO led to a strong decrease in L5s (0.61±0.02 L5s per column; Figure 3V–W; ****p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3V-W.

claims.claim: Dcp-1 positive apoptotic cells are observed in the most proximal row of the lamina when both spi and Col4a1 are knocked down in xgO.
claims.source: Under these conditions we also observed Dcp-1 positive apoptotic cells in the most proximal row of the lamina, which were never observed in controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) but were observed when L5 differentiation was blocked above (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: xgO-derived Spi and Col4a1 are both necessary and sufficient to induce L5 differentiation.
claims.source: Thus, xgO-derived Spi and Col4a1 are both necessary and sufficient to induce L5 differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi and overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: xgO secrete multiple factors that lead to activation of the MAPK cascade in the proximal lamina to induce differentiation of L5s.
claims.source: Altogether, we found that xgO secrete multiple factors that lead to activation of the MAPK cascade in the proximal lamina to induce differentiation of L5s.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: A gradient of Hh signalling activity in lamina columns specifies L1-L5 identities such that high levels specify L2 and L3 identities, intermediate levels specify L1 and L4 identities, and low levels specify L5 identity.
claims.source: We recently showed that a gradient of Hh signalling activity in lamina columns specifies L1-L5 identities such that high levels specify L2 and L3 (distal cell) identities, intermediate levels specify L1 and L4 (intermediate cell) identities, and low levels specify L5 (proximal cell) identity (Bostock et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Overexpressing spi and Col4a1 in xgO results in ectopic L5 neurons.
claims.source: Since overexpressing spi and Col4a1 in the xgO resulted in ectopic L5 neurons, we wondered what the source of these ectopic cells was.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: There is no decrease in the number of L1-L3s or L4s per column when either spi or Col4a1 is overexpressed in xgO.
claims.source: We quantified other lamina neuron types when either spi or Col4a1 was overexpressed in xgO and found no decrease in the number of L1-L3s (Slp2-only expressing cells) or L4s (Bsh-only expressing cells) per column compared to controls (Figure 3S).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3S.

claims.claim: Ectopic L5s are not produced at the expense of other lamina neuron types.
claims.source: Thus, ectopic L5s were not produced at the expense of other lamina neuron types.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the quantification data.

claims.claim: The 'extra' LPCs are specified with L5 identity through low Hh signalling activity in the proximal lamina.
claims.source: We hypothesised that though fated to die, 'extra' LPCs are specified with L5 identity through low Hh signalling activity in the proximal lamina, and that the overexpression of Spi and Col4a1 in xgO generated ectopic L5s by inducing differentiation and survival of the 'extra' LPCs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a hypothesis based on previous findings and current observations.

claims.claim: Hyperactivating MAPK signalling in the lamina leads to premature neuronal differentiation.
claims.source: As reported previously, hyperactivating MAPK signalling in the lamina led to premature neuronal differentiation: instead of sequential differentiation of L1-L4, seen as a triangular front, most lamina columns differentiated simultaneously ( (Figure 4) , Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C; Fernandes et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C, as well as a citation.

claims.claim: No LPCs remain undifferentiated past lamina column 5 when MAPK signalling is hyperactivated, including the row of cells that normally correspond to the 'extra' LPCs.
claims.source: We observed no LPCs that remained undifferentiated (Dac+ and Elav-) past lamina column 5, including the row of cells that normally correspond to the 'extra' LPCs (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C.

claims.claim: There is a concomitant decrease in cleaved Dcp-1 positive cells when MAPK signalling is hyperactivated in the lamina.
claims.source: Importantly, we also observed a concomitant decrease in cleaved Dcp-1 positive cells (Figure 4C and E ; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test), suggesting that forcing the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate blocked their death.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claims.claim: Forcing the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate blocks their death.
claims.source: Importantly, we also observed a concomitant decrease in cleaved Dcp-1 positive cells (Figure 4C and E ; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test), suggesting that forcing the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate blocked their death.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Two rows of cells co-expressing Slp2 and Bsh are often observed in the proximal lamina when neuronal differentiation is forced.
claims.source: Next, we examined the distribution of lamina neuron types when we forced neuronal differentiation. We often observed two rows of cells co-expressing Slp2 and Bsh in the proximal lamina (Figure 4B and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, D), indicating the presence of ectopic L5s.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B, D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, D.

claims.claim: The average number of L5s per column is approximately 1.4-fold higher in laminas in which differentiation is ectopically induced compared with controls.
claims.source: While there was no significant difference between the average number of L1-L3s or L4s per column, the average number of L5s per column was ~1.4-fold higher in laminas in which differentiation was ectopically induced compared with controls, that is, they contained 1.4±0.08 L5s per column compared to 1.00±0.05 L5s per column in controls (Figure 4B, D and F–G; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney U-test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B, D and F-G.

claims.claim: Hyperactivating MAPK signalling in the lamina drives ectopic differentiation of L5 neurons.
claims.source: Thus, hyperactivating MAPK signalling in the lamina drove ectopic differentiation of L5 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Ectopic L5s are only observed in the proximal but never in the distal lamina when MAPK signalling is hyperactivated.
claims.source: Importantly, ectopic L5s were only observed in the proximal but never in the distal lamina (Figure 4D, N=18/18; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, N=9/9).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The absence of cell death in the row distal to L5s and the presence of ectopic L5s in this row indicate that hyperactivating MAPK signalling induces the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate into L5s.
claims.source: Taken together, the absence of cell death in the row distal to L5s and the presence of ectopic L5s in this row indicate that hyperactivating MAPK signalling induces the 'extra' LPCs to differentiate into L5s.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The 'extra' LPCs are specified as L5s though fated to die normally.
claims.source: Thus, the 'extra' LPCs are specified as L5s though fated to die normally.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Lamina precursors are specified by Hh signalling prior to differentiation.
claims.source: These data are consistent with our work showing that lamina precursors are specified by Hh signalling prior to differentiation and that the most proximal cells, which experience the lowest levels of Hh pathway activity and are specified as L5s (Bostock et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: More LPCs are specified as L5s than differentiate normally.
claims.source: Importantly, the presence of ectopic L5s when differentiation is induced demonstrates that more LPCs are specified as L5s than differentiate normally.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Cleaved Dcp-1 is absent in homozygous DroncI24 animals, confirming that apoptosis is blocked.
claims.source: We tested whether the 'extra' LPCs differentiated as L5s when apoptosis was blocked in animals mutant for Death regulator Nedd2-like caspase (Dronc), an initiator caspase essential for caspase-dependent cell death (Fuchs and Steller, 2011). Cleaved Dcp-1 was absent in homozygous DroncI24 animals confirming that apoptosis was blocked (Figure 5A; N=26/26; with full penetrance).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Cells that are positive for Dac but negative for Elav are detected between L1-L4 and L5 neurons past column 5 in DroncI24 animals, which are never observed in controls.
claims.source: Indeed, we detected cells that were positive for the lamina marker Dachshund (Dac) but negative for the pan-neuronal marker Elav between L1-L4 and L5 neurons past column 5, which were never observed in controls (Figure 5A compared to Figure 4A; N=13/13; with full penetrance).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A compared to Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The 'extra' LPCs retained when apoptosis is blocked do not express lamina neuron-type markers Slp2 or Bsh.
claims.source: These cells did not express lamina neuron-type markers Slp2 or Bsh, which L5s co-express and which individually label L1-L3s and L4s, respectively (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: Although the 'extra' LPCs are retained when apoptosis is blocked, they do not differentiate into neurons.
claims.source: Thus, although the 'extra' LPCs were retained when apoptosis was blocked, they did not differentiate into neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Ectopic L5s are observed only when all LPCs are forced to differentiate, bypassing the need for differentiation signals from glia, but not when apoptosis is blocked.
claims.source: We observed ectopic L5s only when all LPCs were forced to differentiate, bypassing the need for differentiation signals from glia, but not when apoptosis was blocked (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D, and Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from comparing different experimental conditions.

claims.claim: The 'extra' LPCs, though specified as L5s, do not receive differentiation signals from xgO in Dronc mutants or in the wild-type.
claims.source: This suggests that the 'extra' LPCs, though specified as L5s, did not receive differentiation signals from xgO in Dronc mutants or in the wild-type, where failing to differentiate they were eliminated by apoptosis.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The most proximal row of LPCs fated to differentiate into L5s is the row nearest to xgO, and therefore, the first to receive differentiation signals.
claims.source: How are only half of the LPCs specified as L5s chosen to differentiate in an invariant manner? The most proximal row of LPCs fated to differentiate into L5s is the row nearest to xgO, and therefore, the first to receive differentiation signals.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the tissue architecture.

claims.claim: Newly induced L5s may limit the ability of more distal LPCs to differentiate by preventing MAPK activation in neighbouring cells.
claims.source: We speculated that newly induced L5s may then limit the ability of more distal LPCs to differentiate, by preventing MAPK activation in neighbouring cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a speculation based on the observations.

claims.claim: Argos (Aos) is a transcriptional target of MAPK signalling and a secreted antagonist of the EGF Spi.
claims.source: Aos is a transcriptional target of MAPK signalling and a secreted antagonist of the EGF Spi (Freeman et al., 1992; Golembo et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claims.claim: aos-lacZ is expressed in xgO and differentiating lamina neurons, with the highest levels detected in L5s.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we examined argos (aos) expression with an enhancer trap in the aos locus, aosW11. aos-lacZ (aosW11/+) was expressed in xgO and differentiating lamina neurons, with the highest levels detected in L5s (Figure 5D–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claims.claim: Ectopic L5s are noted in the laminas of aosW11 heterozygotes.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also noted ectopic L5s in the laminas of aosW11 heterozygotes, which could be the result of decreased Aos expression, as aosW11 is a hypomorphic loss-of-function allele (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Knocking down aos in developing L5s results in a statistically significant approximately 1.2-fold increase in the number of L5s relative to controls.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we knocked down aos by RNAi using a driver expressed specifically in developing L5s (Jenett et al., 2012; Figure 5G). We observed a statistically significant ~1.2-fold increase in the number of L5s relative to controls, that is, 0.99±0.02 L5s per column compared to 0.83±0.01 L5s per column in controls (Figure 5F–H; p<0.0005, Mann-Whitney U-test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claims.claim: xgO induce MAPK activity in the most proximal LPCs, resulting in their differentiation and in the production of the feedback inhibitor Aos.
claims.source: Altogether, our data indicate a model in which xgO induce MAPK activity in the most proximal LPCs, resulting in their differentiation and in the production of the feedback inhibitor Aos.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Aos limits further differentiation in the column by fine-tuning the availability of the differentiation signal Spi.
claims.source: In turn, Aos limits further differentiation in the column by fine-tuning the availability of the differentiation signal Spi, which ensures that only one L5 differentiates per column, and determines the final number of neurons in each lamina column.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Each lamina unit or column in the adult is composed of exactly five neurons.
claims.source: In Drosophila, photoreceptors induce their target field, the lamina, thus, establishing retinotopy between the compound eye and the lamina (Huang and Kunes, 1996). Each lamina unit or column in the adult is composed of exactly five neurons; however, columns initially contain six LPCs.

results.result: Each lamina column initially contains approximately 6 post-mitotic lamina precursor cells (LPCs), but only 5 differentiate into neurons (L1-L5). The sixth 'extra' LPC, invariantly positioned above the L5 neuron, undergoes apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5, C26, C103-C104 collectively establish the basic architecture of lamina development. The claims are supported by direct observations (Figure 1A schematic, Figure 2 showing Dcp-1 staining in the 'extra' cell position) and are consistent with established knowledge of Drosophila visual system development. The stereotyped position and fate of the 'extra' LPC is well-documented.

results.result: EGFR activity in the outer chiasm giant glia (xgO) is required for L5 neuronal differentiation. Blocking EGFR signaling specifically in xgO leads to a dramatic and specific reduction in L5 neurons without affecting xgO morphology or other lamina neuron types.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C37 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including genetic screens (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-M), temporal control experiments using Gal80ts (C33), cell-type specific quantifications (C35, Figure 1G-I), and adult phenotype analysis (C36). The specificity of the phenotype and appropriate controls strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: When EGFR signaling is blocked in xgO, LPC formation and column assembly occur normally in young columns, but LPCs that fail to differentiate into L5s undergo apoptosis in older columns, as evidenced by increased Dcp-1 positive cells in the proximal lamina.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are supported by quantitative data showing normal LPC numbers in columns 1-4 (Figure 2C) but decreased numbers in older columns, along with significantly increased Dcp-1 positive cells specifically in the proximal row (Figure 2A-D). The temporal progression and spatial specificity of apoptosis support the interpretation that undifferentiated proximal LPCs die.

results.result: Photoreceptor-derived EGF is required for L5 differentiation, and xgO respond to EGF from photoreceptors to relay signals that induce differentiation of proximal LPCs into L5 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by experiments using rho3 mutants (which cannot secrete EGF from photoreceptor axons) showing loss of L5s (Figure 3A, C), and rescue experiments restoring Rho3 specifically in photoreceptors (Figure 3B, C). The logic connecting photoreceptor EGF to xgO signaling is sound given that blocking EGFR in xgO phenocopies loss of photoreceptor EGF.

results.result: xgO secrete Spi and Col4a1 in response to EGFR activity. These ligands are expressed in xgO under physiological conditions and can rescue L5 differentiation when co-expressed with EGFRDN in xgO.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C58 are supported by a systematic ligand screen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), validation of ligand expression using Gal4 drivers and in situ HCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-I), rescue experiments (Figure 3F-K, P), and demonstration that ligand expression is EGFR-dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L-O). The exclusion of false positives (bnl, ths) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: LPCs express the receptors EGFR and Ddr throughout the lamina, making them competent to respond to Spi and Col4a1 from xgO. Expressing these ligands in xgO rescues dpMAPK signaling in L5s, and co-expression produces enhanced rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 are supported by expression analysis using Gal4 drivers and in situ HCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1P-Q), previous literature on EGFR expression (C61), and functional rescue of dpMAPK signaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1R-T). The additive effect of co-expressing both ligands (Figure 3L-P) supports their cooperative function.

results.result: Overexpressing Spi or Col4a1 in xgO is sufficient to induce ectopic L5 differentiation, resulting in approximately 19-24% increases in L5 numbers per column.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by quantitative data from overexpression experiments (Figure 3Q-S) with appropriate statistical analysis. The modest but significant increases in L5 numbers demonstrate sufficiency of these ligands for inducing L5 differentiation.

results.result: xgO-derived Spi and Col4a1 are both necessary and sufficient to induce L5 differentiation. Knocking down both ligands simultaneously in xgO leads to a strong decrease in L5s and appearance of apoptotic cells in the proximal lamina.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by RNAi experiments using validated lines (Figure 3T-W). The observation that simultaneous knockdown produces a stronger phenotype than individual knockdowns, along with appearance of Dcp-1 positive cells in the proximal row (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), demonstrates necessity. Combined with sufficiency data (C64-C66), this establishes that these ligands are both necessary and sufficient.

results.result: When MAPK signaling is hyperactivated in the lamina, ectopic L5 neurons differentiate specifically in the proximal lamina (approximately 1.4-fold increase), apoptosis is reduced, and the 'extra' LPCs differentiate into L5s. This demonstrates that more LPCs are specified as L5s than normally differentiate.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C86, C88 are supported by experiments using MAPKACT or PntP1 overexpression (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The key observations include: premature differentiation (C77), absence of undifferentiated LPCs past column 5 (C78), decreased Dcp-1 positive cells (C79), two rows of Slp2+Bsh+ cells (C81), quantitative increase in L5s but not other neuron types (C82), and spatial restriction to proximal lamina (C84). The logic connecting these observations to the conclusion that 'extra' LPCs are specified as L5s is sound.

results.result: When apoptosis is blocked in Dronc mutants, the 'extra' LPCs are retained but do not differentiate into neurons. This suggests that 'extra' LPCs are specified as L5s but do not receive differentiation signals from xgO.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 are supported by analysis of DroncI24 mutants showing absence of Dcp-1 (C89), retention of Dac+Elav- cells between L1-L4 and L5 (C90), absence of differentiation markers (C91), and normal differentiation of other neuron types (C106, Figure 5B). The interpretation that these cells are specified as L5s but fail to receive differentiation signals is reasonable given the forced differentiation experiments (C93).

results.result: The most proximal row of LPCs differentiates first into L5s because they are nearest to xgO. Newly induced L5s secrete the Spi antagonist Argos (Aos) to limit MAPK activation in neighboring 'extra' LPCs, preventing their differentiation. Knocking down aos in L5s increases L5 numbers by approximately 1.2-fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C102 are supported by aos-lacZ expression analysis showing high levels in L5s (Figure 5D-E), observation of ectopic L5s in aos hypomorphic heterozygotes (C99), and RNAi experiments showing increased L5 numbers when aos is knocked down in developing L5s (Figure 5F-H). The model of feedback inhibition through Aos is well-supported by the data and consistent with known Aos function as a Spi antagonist (C97).

results.result: The authors define a unique strategy for setting neuronal numbers: regulating how many precursors from a larger pool are induced to differentiate, followed by programmed cell death of excess precursors. The stereotyped pattern arises from tissue architecture and feedback from differentiating neurons rather than intrinsic programming.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108, C116, C122-C123 represent the major conceptual conclusions of the work. These are well-supported by the collective evidence showing: (1) twice as many LPCs are specified as L5s than differentiate (C107, supported by forced differentiation experiments), (2) tissue architecture determines which cells receive signals first (C110, C116), and (3) feedback from newly differentiated L5s limits further differentiation (C101-C102). The distinction from intrinsic programming is supported by the Dronc mutant experiments (C121-C122).

results.result: L5 neuronal differentiation proceeds in the youngest columns despite Aos secretion by newly induced L5s. Differentiating L5s express aos at low levels initially and increase expression gradually until it plateaus from column 5 onwards, which may enable differentiation of the youngest LPCs while inhibiting the row immediately distal.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 are supported by quantitative analysis of aos-lacZ expression as a function of column age (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). The observation of gradual increase in aos expression provides a mechanistic explanation for how ongoing L5 differentiation can occur despite feedback inhibition. However, C115 is somewhat speculative as it proposes a mechanism without direct functional testing.

results.result: In addition to wrapping glia, xgO also receive and relay signals from photoreceptors to induce neuronal differentiation in the lamina. This is the first functional role ascribed to xgO, which are born from central brain neuroblasts and migrate into the optic lobes.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 are supported by the experimental data showing xgO function (C117, Figure 1E-F) and citations regarding xgO origin and migration (C119). The novelty claim (C118) is reasonable given the lack of prior functional studies on xgO. This represents an important discovery about glial coordination of development.

results.result: In the lamina, MAPK-induced neuronal differentiation and cell survival are intimately linked. LPCs that do not activate MAPK signaling sufficiently do not differentiate and are eliminated by apoptosis. The xgO-secreted ligands Spi and Col4a1 function as both differentiation signals and trophic factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126 are supported by the observation that blocking differentiation signals leads to apoptosis (Figure 2), and that forcing differentiation prevents apoptosis (Figure 4). The dual role interpretation (C126) is reasonable given that the same signals (Spi, Col4a1) both induce differentiation and promote survival. The connection to Head involution defective (C125) is speculative but supported by citations.

results.result: Background claims establishing the developmental context of Drosophila visual system development, including photoreceptor differentiation, lamina induction, and the role of Hedgehog and EGF signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C29 represent background information from the introduction, supported by citations to previous literature. These establish the developmental context for the current work and are consistent with established knowledge in the field. While important for framing the study, these are not novel findings of this manuscript.

results.result: The outer chiasm giant glia (xgO) reside below the lamina and secrete multiple ligands to induce L5 differentiation in response to EGF from photoreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 summarize key findings that are elaborated in detail elsewhere. C6 is supported by imaging data (Figure 1E), and C7 is supported by the ligand screen and rescue experiments (Figure 3). These claims are well-supported but represent summary statements of results detailed in other claim groups.

results.result: Two precursors are specified as L5s but only one differentiates during normal development. The row of precursors nearest to xgO differentiate into L5s and antagonize differentiation signaling to prevent the 'extra' precursors from differentiating.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 represent summary statements of major findings detailed elsewhere. C8-C9 are supported by the forced differentiation experiments (Figure 4), C10 is supported by tissue architecture and experimental observations, and C11 is supported by the Aos experiments (Figure 5). These are well-supported summary claims.

results.result: A gradient of Hh signaling activity in lamina columns specifies L1-L5 identities, with low levels specifying L5 identity in the most proximal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C72 and C87 cite previous work by the same authors (Bostock et al., 2022) establishing the role of Hh signaling in LPC specification. This provides important context for interpreting the current findings but is not a novel result of this manuscript. The claims are supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: The 'extra' LPCs did not differentiate when apoptosis was blocked but generated ectopic L5s when forced to differentiate. It is more likely that the 'extra' cells are specified as L5s but that other mechanisms restricted their differentiation in Dronc mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 are supported by comparison of Dronc mutant phenotypes (Figure 5A-B) with forced differentiation phenotypes (Figure 4D). The interpretation in C106 is reasonable given that other lamina neuron types differentiate normally in Dronc mutants, suggesting the block is specific to the 'extra' cells rather than a general mis-specification.

results.result: xgO secrete Spi and Col4a1 that activate MAPK signaling in LPCs. Due to tissue architecture, signals reach the most proximal row first, which differentiate and secrete Aos to limit Spi availability, preventing MAPK activation in 'extra' L5 LPCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 represent summary statements from the Discussion that integrate multiple findings. C109 is supported by the ligand identification experiments (Figure 3), C110 is inferred from tissue architecture, C111 is supported by Aos expression and RNAi data (Figure 5), and C112 is supported by the model shown in Figure 6. These are well-supported integrative conclusions.

results.result: In the lamina, although the LPCs eliminated by programmed cell death are identifiable and the process stereotyped, it does not appear to be linked to an intrinsic programme.
results.evaluation: Claim C121 is supported by the collective evidence showing that the stereotyped pattern of apoptosis depends on extrinsic signals (xgO-derived ligands) and feedback (Aos from L5s) rather than cell-autonomous programming. The Dronc mutant experiments showing that 'extra' cells can be retained without differentiating (Figure 5A-C) support this interpretation.

results.result: Col4a1 may perform dual roles by promoting MAPK activity directly through its receptor Ddr, and perhaps also by limiting Spi diffusivity to aid in localizing MAPK activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 is explicitly speculative ('may perform dual roles', 'perhaps also'). While the first role (promoting MAPK through Ddr) is supported by the rescue experiments and receptor expression data, the second proposed role (limiting Spi diffusivity) is not directly tested. This represents a reasonable hypothesis for future investigation but lacks experimental support in the current manuscript.
